title: 2026 Social Policy Awards: Best Article Award
text:
The article “Do Support Mechanisms Ensure a Smooth Labor Market Transition? A Cross-Cultural Qualitative Study on Vocational High School Graduates in Türkiye”, co-authored by our founding board members Professor Dr Volkan Işık and Professor Dr Mustafa Çağlar Özdemir with Research Assistant Dr Bünyamin Yasin Çakmak, has received the Best Article Award in the Article Category of the Social Policy Research Association’s 2026 Social Policy Awards.
The award was presented at the 25th Congress of Labour Economics and Industrial Relations, hosted by Aydın Adnan Menderes University.
The research examines the transition into the labour market of Turkish and Syrian students and graduates of vocational and technical secondary education. It draws on interviews with 154 stakeholders in five provinces. The study explores mismatches between vocational education and labour market expectations, employer attitudes and the effects of employment support. It offers policy recommendations to strengthen school–employer cooperation and align vocational education more closely with industry needs.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
text:
ÇAHSPAR is an academic association established to strengthen scientific research, academic collaboration and social impact in working life and social policy.
Our association aims to bring together academics from different universities and disciplines who study working life, social policy and related topics, and to improve the quality, diversity and international visibility of scientific knowledge produced in Türkiye.
ÇAHSPAR’s approach extends academic activity beyond individual research and university boundaries. Sharing knowledge, building lasting research partnerships, supporting early-career researchers, developing national and international networks and connecting research with society are central to our work.

Our association aims to bring together academics from different universities and disciplines who study working life, social policy and related topics, and to improve the quality, diversity and international visibility of scientific knowledge produced in Türkiye.
ÇAHSPAR’s approach extends academic activity beyond individual research and university boundaries. Sharing knowledge, building lasting research partnerships, supporting early-career researchers, developing national and international networks and connecting research with society are central to our work.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
text:
Why ÇAHSPAR?
Türkiye has a substantial body of academic expertise in working life and social policy. Researchers at many universities undertake valuable studies on employment relations, employment, labour markets, social security, social policy, migration, youth, education, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, sustainability, social entrepreneurship and social change.
However, much of this work can remain within individual researchers’ and institutions’ academic circles. Potential partnerships between universities, disciplines and research groups may remain underdeveloped.
ÇAHSPAR aims to provide a platform for connection, collaboration and visibility.
Our purpose goes beyond bringing academics together under one roof. We aim to build a sustainable ecosystem where researchers know one another’s work, develop joint research and national and international projects, and where early-career academics can engage with experienced researchers. We also seek stronger links between research in Türkiye and the international academic community.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
section: An Initiative Founded by Nine Academics
text:
An Initiative Founded by Nine Academics
ÇAHSPAR emerged as a joint initiative of nine academics with different backgrounds and research interests.
They shared a belief that Türkiye’s strong academic potential in working life and social policy could be supported through greater interaction, collaboration and international connections.
By bringing their expertise together, these nine academics seek to develop their own research and contribute to a wider research community.
ÇAHSPAR is therefore independent of any single university, discipline or narrowly defined research area. We aim to be an open and inclusive academic platform connecting institutions, disciplines, research approaches and generations of researchers.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
section: Bringing Research from Türkiye to the International Community
text:
Bringing Research from Türkiye to the International Community
One of ÇAHSPAR’s key objectives is to make research produced in Türkiye on working life and social policy more visible and accessible internationally.
Türkiye’s distinctive experiences, rapid social and economic transformation and diverse policy practices make it an important setting for international research in these fields.
Research conducted in Türkiye therefore offers valuable insights for both national scholarship and global academic debate.
Through international conferences, academic networks, research partnerships, joint publications, international projects, workshops and other academic platforms, ÇAHSPAR aims to help researchers in Türkiye build stronger connections with the global academic ecosystem.
Our goal is both to share knowledge produced in Türkiye with the world and to strengthen researchers’ access to international academic expertise.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
text:
National and International Networks
Building networks and participating in existing ones are central to ÇAHSPAR’s approach to academic development.
We aim to strengthen communication between academics, researchers, universities, research centres, public bodies, civil society organisations and other stakeholders working on working life and social policy in Türkiye.
Developing connections with universities, research centres, professional and academic organisations and international networks across Europe and the wider world is also a priority.
We want these networks to support knowledge sharing, joint research, project development, academic mobility, joint publications, early-career researchers and new research agendas.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
text:
Growing the Ecosystem Together
One of ÇAHSPAR’s most important long-term goals is to build a broad working life and social policy research ecosystem that extends beyond its own activities.
Academics are at its centre, alongside early-career researchers, doctoral students, research centres, universities, public bodies, international organisations, civil society organisations and other stakeholders in working life.
Working life and social policy are academic fields that also directly affect millions of people’s everyday lives, working conditions, social security, wellbeing and futures.
Strengthening the connection between scientific knowledge and practice is therefore a core priority.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
section: A Meeting Place for Early-Career Researchers
text:
A Meeting Place for Early-Career Researchers
ÇAHSPAR places particular emphasis on the academic development of early-career academics and researchers.
We aim to create an environment where doctoral students and researchers at the start of their careers can meet experienced academics, share their research, receive feedback and access national and international academic networks.
We measure ÇAHSPAR’s long-term success through both our current work and the academic networks and culture of collaboration we pass on to future researchers.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
text:
From Research to Social Impact
We believe that the value of scientific research extends beyond academic publications.
Sharing knowledge about working life and social policy with policymakers, public bodies, workers’ and employers’ organisations, civil society and different sections of society increases its social value.
Alongside producing research, ÇAHSPAR therefore places emphasis on sharing, discussing and translating scientific knowledge into public benefit.
Through academic meetings, workshops, conferences, research groups, training, publications and communications, we aim to build stronger connections between academic knowledge, society and practice.

title: About ÇAHSPAR
text:
ÇAHSPAR’s Vision for the Future
ÇAHSPAR’s vision is an academic ecosystem recognised nationally and internationally, where researchers in Türkiye working on working life and social policy know one another, work together and maintain strong global connections.
In the coming period, we aim to:

Increase academic collaboration among researchers in Türkiye
Encourage interdisciplinary research
Support the development of national and international research projects
Strengthen participation in international academic networks
Increase the international visibility of research produced in Türkiye
Support early-career researchers’ academic development
Contribute to new research agendas in working life and social policy
Strengthen interaction between scientific knowledge, public bodies, society and practice


More Than an Association
We see ÇAHSPAR as an academic foundation for thinking, researching and producing knowledge together.
What began as a joint initiative by nine academics will grow through participation by researchers from universities and disciplines across Türkiye, building strong links with international academic networks beyond national borders.
We believe that a stronger academic future for working life and social policy depends on producing research, sharing knowledge, connecting researchers and bringing Türkiye’s academic expertise to the world.
ÇAHSPAR was founded to build this shared future together, for fairer working lives and a fairer society.

title: ÇAHSPAR Index
text:
The ÇAHSPAR Working Life and Social Policy Index is an original initiative designed to monitor developments in working life, social policy and social welfare through multidimensional indicators.
It aims to track Türkiye’s working life and social policy landscape regularly by considering job quality, employment, social protection, equality, welfare, sustainability and the future of work together.

title: ÇAHSPAR Index
text:
The ÇAHSPAR Working Life and Social Policy Index is an original initiative designed to monitor developments in working life, social policy and social welfare through multidimensional indicators.
It aims to track Türkiye’s working life and social policy landscape regularly by considering job quality, employment, social protection, equality, welfare, sustainability and the future of work together.

title: ÇAHSPAR Index
text:
Purpose of the Index
The index’s main purpose is to reveal developments in working life and social policy through measurable, comparable and trackable indicators.
Its objectives include:

Monitoring developments in working life
Assessing changes in social policy
Bringing together indicators of workers’ and society’s wellbeing
Identifying changes over time
Providing a reliable information source for researchers, decision-makers, public bodies and civil society organisations

title: ÇAHSPAR Index
text:
Dimensions of the Index
The methodology will bring together key working life and social policy indicators under several dimensions.

Working Life
Employment, unemployment, working conditions, wages and key labour market indicators.


Social Policy
Indicators of social protection, social security, social services and social policy practices.


Equality and Inclusion
Participation in working life by women, young people and different groups of workers, alongside workplace equality indicators.


Welfare
Indicators of income, poverty, living conditions and social welfare.


Sustainability
Sustainable working lives, social sustainability and the future of work.


The Future of Work
Digital transformation, artificial intelligence, automation, new forms of work and technological change in working life.

title: ÇAHSPAR Index
text:
Data Sources
The index is expected to draw on reliable and comparable national and international data sources.
Key sources will include:
TurkStat (TÜİK) · Social Security Institution (SGK) · Ministry of Labour and Social Security (ÇSGB) · ILO · OECD · Eurostat · World Bank · United Nations
alongside other relevant institutional data sources.

title: ÇAHSPAR Index
text:
Methodology
The methodological framework will cover indicator selection, data standardisation, the construction of dimensions and index calculation.
The methodology, data sources and calculation procedures will be made public so that results are transparent, traceable and reproducible.

title: Our Story
text:
We are nine academics who have spent around 20 years producing work together, debating and learning from one another across different universities in labour economics, industrial relations and social policy.
During these years, we have contributed to numerous national and international books, articles, research studies and projects. Our experiences in different universities, academic environments and research fields have made one point increasingly clear: knowledge about working life and social policy needs to reach beyond academia. It must be produced and shared with close attention to current developments, social needs and the future.
We believe in connecting scientific knowledge with everyday life. While addressing Türkiye’s working life and social policy challenges in their distinctive context, we also follow global developments closely. We believe in supporting high-quality academic work and researchers who can contribute to debate nationally and internationally.
For a long time, we had discussed a shared ambition: to create an environment where academics, early-career researchers, students and everyone committed to these fields could meet, discuss ideas freely, strengthen a culture of joint research and connect with national and international academic networks.
ÇAHSPAR emerged as a concrete expression of that ambition.
We came together again to pool the academic experience we had built over the years, support new researchers, strengthen scientific output in working life and social policy and become part of a stronger academic ecosystem connecting Türkiye with the world.
We envisage ÇAHSPAR as a platform for research and academic work, and as an environment for thinking, creating, sharing and developing knowledge together.
Drawing on our experience, we look towards the future and set out to produce stronger, higher-quality and more influential research in working life and social policy.
We know that knowledge grows when it is shared, and ideas develop when we create them together.

title: Constitution
text:
2. Purpose, Activities and Scope
Article 2 – The association was established to improve the quality of working and social life through innovative, sustainable, not-for-profit research, training, projects and consultancy in working life and social policy.
Within this scope, the association aims to develop sustainable solutions in decent work, social protection, employment, gender equality, environmental awareness and social policy.
The association’s activities and methods are as follows:

Undertake training, research, public opinion research, projects and academic studies nationally and internationally.
Organise and deliver all forms of certified training, including courses, seminars, conferences, panels and information sessions.
Collaborate with national and international institutions and organisations and establish research and project platforms.
Join and obtain accreditation from national and international umbrella organisations established for purposes consistent with its own, and accredit national associations.
Obtain necessary information, records, documents and publications; establish a documentation centre; and provide information and publications on employment, working life and social policy.
Publish an academic journal and support scholarly work.
Organise academic events such as congresses, workshops and conferences.
Establish foundations, federations and institutes where necessary.
Provide a healthy working environment and manage matters relating to necessary technical tools, equipment and property.
Establish funds and similar assistance mechanisms to meet members’ basic needs.
Undertake fundraising with the necessary permission, and accept donations and voluntary services.
Establish and make available club premises and social and cultural facilities for members.
Organise meetings, concerts, exhibitions, sports, trips and recreational activities to develop social relationships among members.
Establish branches and representative offices where necessary.

The association’s scope covers all forms of training, research, consultancy and project activities relating to working life and social policy in Türkiye and abroad.

title: Constitution
section: 3. Eligibility for Membership and Membership Procedures

3. Eligibility for Membership and Membership Procedures
Article 3 – Anyone who meets the conditions specified in the Law on Associations, accepts the association’s purposes and principles and agrees to work towards them may apply for membership.
The association has the following membership categories:

Full membership
Honorary membership
Membership of honour

Full membership: Academics, researchers, specialists, employers, natural persons and legal entities with legal capacity who accept the association’s purposes and principles and meet the statutory conditions are entitled to become members.
Honorary membership: By decision of the Board of Directors, honorary membership may be granted to people who show a close interest in the association, have undertaken significant work or have contributed to fields related to its purpose.
Membership of honour: People who have made significant material and non-material contributions to the association may be admitted as members of honour by decision of the Board of Directors.
Article 4 – Applications submitted to the association’s chair shall be accepted or rejected by the Board of Directors within thirty days at the latest. Applicants shall be informed of the outcome in writing.
The association’s full members consist of its founders and those admitted by decision of the Board of Directors following an application.

title: Constitution
text:
4. Members’ Rights and Duties
Article 5 – Members have equal rights. Each member has one vote at the General Assembly. Honorary members do not have voting rights.
Members shall pay the admission fee and monthly or annual subscriptions determined by the General Assembly.

title: Constitution
section: 5. Resignation, Expulsion and Termination of Membership
text:
5. Resignation, Expulsion and Termination of Membership
Article 6 – Every member has the right to resign by written notice. Resignation is considered complete when the notice reaches the Board of Directors.
Article 7 – The following constitute grounds for expulsion:

Acting contrary to the association’s constitution
Persistently avoiding assigned duties
Failing to pay subscriptions within six months despite a warning
Failing to comply with decisions of the association’s governing bodies
No longer meeting the conditions for membership
Prolonged inactivity due to ill health, old age, detention or similar reasons

Where any of these circumstances is established, the member shall be expelled by decision of the Board of Directors.
Article 8 – Membership terminates automatically in the following circumstances:

The member’s death
The member’s resignation
Loss of the capacity to exercise civil rights
The emergence of a legal impediment to membership or loss of the required qualifications

title: Constitution
text:
6. Governing Bodies
Article 9 – The association’s governing bodies are:

The General Assembly
The Board of Directors
The Supervisory Board

title: Constitution
text:
7. General Assembly
Article 10 – The General Assembly is the association’s highest decision-making body. It consists of registered members and, where applicable, branch or representative office delegates and elected delegates.
The General Assembly holds ordinary and extraordinary meetings.
The ordinary General Assembly meets every three years in June. An extraordinary General Assembly is convened when deemed necessary by the Board of Directors or Supervisory Board, or upon the written request of one fifth of members.
Members entitled to attend shall be invited at least fifteen days before the meeting. The date, time, venue and agenda shall be announced appropriately. If the first meeting does not achieve a quorum, a second meeting may be held.
The General Assembly requires an absolute majority of members entitled to attend; a two-thirds majority is required for constitutional amendments and dissolution.
Each member has one vote at the General Assembly and must vote in person. Legal entities vote through a representative.

title: Constitution
section: 8. Duties and Powers of the General Assembly
text:
8. Duties and Powers of the General Assembly
Article 11 – The General Assembly’s duties and powers are:

Electing the association’s governing bodies
Amending the constitution
Discussing reports of the Board of Directors and Supervisory Board
Approving the budget
Supervising governing bodies and removing them from office where necessary
Approving property purchases, sales and similar significant decisions
Deciding on admission to and expulsion from membership
Deciding on joining or leaving a federation
Authorising the opening and closure of branches and representative offices
Deciding on dissolution and liquidation

title: Constitution
text:
9. Board of Directors
Article 12 – The Board of Directors is elected by the General Assembly and consists of five principal and five substitute members.
At its first meeting, the Board allocates responsibilities and appoints a chair, deputy chair, general secretary, treasurer and accounting officer.
The Board is the association’s executive body. It represents the association in its affairs, takes decisions and implements them.
Its duties include:

Carrying out tasks assigned by the General Assembly
Representing the association or delegating authority to one or more members
Managing income and expenditure accounts
Preparing the budget for the following period and submitting it to the General Assembly
Preparing regulations governing the association’s work
Managing property purchases and sales, leases, pledges and similar transactions
Undertaking procedures to establish branches and representative offices
Preparing activity reports
Deciding on membership applications, rejections and expulsions

title: Constitution
text:
10. Supervisory Board
Article 13 – The Supervisory Board is elected by the General Assembly and consists of three principal and three substitute members.
It examines whether the association’s activities, books and accounts comply with legislation and the constitution. It reports its findings to the Board of Directors and, where necessary, the General Assembly.

title: Constitution
text:
11. Sources of Income
Article 14 – The association’s income sources are:

Membership subscriptions
Branch contributions
Donations and assistance from natural persons and legal entities
Income from tea gatherings, dinners, trips, concerts, competitions, congresses, workshops, conferences and similar events
Income from academic publications and publishing
Income from the association’s assets
Fundraising conducted in accordance with legislation
Profits from commercial activities
Profits from the academic journal
Other income

title: Constitution
text:
12. Bookkeeping Principles and Procedures
Article 15 – The association shall keep its books on the operating account basis. If its annual gross income exceeds the specified threshold, it shall adopt the balance sheet basis.
Books and records shall be maintained in accordance with the Regulation on Associations.
The books to be kept include:

Membership Register
Decision Book
Correspondence Registers
Balance Sheet, Budget and Final Accounts Book
Income and Expenditure Book
Fixed Asset Register
Receipt Register

title: Constitution
text:
13. Income and Expenditure Procedures
Article 16 – Income shall be collected against a receipt. For income collected through a bank, the bank receipt may serve in its place.
Expenditure shall be supported by invoices, till receipts, receipts and similar expenditure documents. Expense vouchers and bank receipts may be used where necessary.

title: Constitution
text:
14. Declaration and Notification Obligations
Article 17 – The association’s activities and income and expenditure transactions for the preceding year shall be declared by the chair to the local administrative authority within the first four months of each calendar year.
Where required, the association shall submit notifications of General Assembly results, property holdings, assistance received from abroad, projects and changes in accordance with legislation.

title: Constitution
text:
15. Internal Audit
Article 18 – Internal audits may be undertaken by the General Assembly, Board of Directors or Supervisory Board. Independent audit organisations may be engaged where necessary.
The Supervisory Board shall audit the association at least once a year and report its findings.

title: Constitution
text:
16. Establishing Representative Offices
Article 19 – The association may establish representative offices where necessary, with authorisation from the General Assembly and a decision of the Board of Directors. Details of the representative and address shall be notified in writing to the local administrative authority.

title: Constitution
text:
17. Branches
Article 20 – The association may establish branches where necessary by decision of the General Assembly. Branches undertake autonomous activities in line with the association’s purposes and services.
The governing bodies of branches are:

The General Assembly
The Board of Directors
The Supervisory Board

title: Constitution
text:
18. Borrowing Procedures
Article 21 – The association may borrow by decision of the Board of Directors where necessary to achieve its purpose and carry out its activities. Borrowing must remain within the association’s income capacity and must not create payment difficulties.

title: Constitution
text:
19. Amending the Constitution
Article 22 – The constitution may be amended by decision of the General Assembly. Amendments require the applicable attendance and voting majorities at the General Assembly.

title: Constitution
text:
20. Dissolution and Liquidation of Assets
Article 23 – The General Assembly may decide to dissolve the association.
The required majority must be achieved for dissolution. Upon dissolution, a liquidation committee consisting of the last members of the Board of Directors shall liquidate the association’s funds, property and rights. Remaining assets shall be transferred to the body designated by the General Assembly or, if none is designated, to the association with the closest purpose.
The full constitution is structured within this framework in respect of the association’s institutional structure, purposes, governance model, membership arrangements and operating principles.
